item.title: “Householder, suppose a vulture, a kite, or a hawk seizes a piece of meat and flies up. Then other vultures, kites, or hawks chase after…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose a vulture, a kite, or a hawk seizes a piece of meat and flies up. Then other vultures, kites, or hawks chase after it, attacking and tearing at that piece of meat. What do you think, householder? If that vulture, kite, or hawk does not quickly let go of that piece of meat, would it thereby meet death or deadly suffering?” “Yes, venerable sir.” … “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom, having abandoned the equanimity based on diversity … he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta

item.title: Where the mind is restrained, There suffering ends. If the mind is fully restrained, One is fully freed from suffering. (The Blessed One): One should…
item.description:
Where the mind is restrained,
There suffering ends.
If the mind is fully restrained,
One is fully freed from suffering.

(The Blessed One):
One should not restrain the mind
Completely in every way.
Do not restrain the mind
When self-control is attained.
Where evil states arise,
There one should restrain the mind.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.24
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s corpse thrown in a charnel ground — with skeleton still connected, still having flesh and blood, held together by…
item.description:
“Furthermore, monks, one sees that woman’s corpse thrown in a charnel ground — with skeleton still connected, still having flesh and blood, held together by sinews … with skeleton still connected, without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews … without flesh, without blood, held together by sinews … disconnected bones scattered here and there — here a hand bone, here a foot bone, here a shin bone, here a thigh bone, here a hip bone, here a back bone, here a skull. What do you think, monks? Has her former charm and beauty disappeared and peril become evident?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “Thus, monks, is the peril in the case of forms.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 13 – Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: Elder Māluṅkyaputta: One who lives heedlessly, Craving grows like a creeper. He drifts and wanders, Life after life, Like a monkey in the forest, Longing…
item.description:
Elder Māluṅkyaputta:

One who lives heedlessly,
Craving grows like a creeper.
He drifts and wanders,
Life after life,
Like a monkey in the forest,
Longing for fruit.

This wretched craving
Poisons the whole world.
When it conquers anyone,
Sorrow increases —
Like birana grass
Spreading and growing.

One who subdues craving,
Wretched, hard to conquer —
Sorrow falls from that person
Like a water drop from a lotus.

You have come here —
I teach this good thing.
Dig up the root of craving
Like seeking the sweet root
Of the usīra grass.
Do not let Māra, the flood,
Destroy you like a reed,
Again and again, forever.

Practice the Buddha’s instruction.
Do not let the moment pass.
If the moment passes, sorrow,
You will suffer in hell.

Heedlessness is dust,
Filthy dust born of heedlessness.
Heedful, with clear wisdom,
Pull out the dart from yourself.

From: Theragāthā 6.5
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Vaṅgīsa: Sensual desire burns me! My mind is on fire. Good indeed, Gotama — Out of compassion, speak The Dhamma that extinguishes the blaze.…
item.description:
Elder Vaṅgīsa:

Sensual desire burns me!
My mind is on fire.
Good indeed, Gotama —
Out of compassion, speak
The Dhamma that extinguishes the blaze.

It is because of distorted perception
That your mind is on fire.
Abandon the sign of the beautiful
That leads to sensual desire.

See formations as impermanent,
Suffering, not-self —
Extinguish great sensual desire —
Do not be burned again and again.
Develop the mind on foulness,
One-pointed, well-concentrated.
Practice mindfulness of the body,
Practice much disenchantment.

Practice the signless,
Destroy the underlying tendency to conceit.
By thoroughly penetrating conceit,
Your practice will be at peace.

From: Theragāthā 21.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Those who live in the world Without restraining sensual desires, Not abandoning passion, Enjoying sensual pleasures — They go to birth and aging, Again and…
item.description:
Those who live in the world
Without restraining sensual desires,
Not abandoning passion,
Enjoying sensual pleasures —
They go to birth and aging,
Again and again,
Bound by craving,
They go with the stream.
Therefore the wise,
Mindful in the world,
Do not enjoy sensual pleasures,
Do not do evil deeds.
Even if they suffer,
Abandoning sensual pleasures,
They are called those
Who go against the stream.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.5

item.title: “Sunakkhatta, suppose there is a bronze cup of drink, beautiful and fragrant, but mixed with poison. Then a man comes who desires to live, not…
item.description:
“Sunakkhatta, suppose there is a bronze cup of drink, beautiful and fragrant, but mixed with poison. Then a man comes who desires to live, not to die, who desires happiness and loathes suffering. What do you think, Sunakkhatta? Would that man drink from that bronze cup if he knew: ‘If I drink from this, I will meet death or deadly suffering’?”
“No, venerable sir.”
“So too, Sunakkhatta, a monk should surely guard himself in regard to the six sense-bases. Knowing that ‘Attachment is the root of suffering,’ he becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment. It does not happen that he would still focus his body on attachment or direct his mind to attachment.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 105 – Sunakkhattasutta

item.title: “Monks, for a monk, those defilements that should be abandoned by direct knowledge have been abandoned by direct knowledge; those defilements that should be abandoned…
item.description:
“Monks, for a monk, those defilements that should be abandoned by direct knowledge have been abandoned by direct knowledge; those defilements that should be abandoned by restraint have been abandoned by restraint … That monk is called one who lives restrained by the restraint of all defilements, who has cut off craving, has shed the fetters, has rightly penetrated conceit, and has made an end of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 2 – Sabbāsavasutta

item.title: “‘I will dwell contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and sorrow in the world.’ Thus, monk, you should…
item.description:
“‘I will dwell contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and sorrow in the world.’ Thus, monk, you should train. Monk, when this concentration of yours is developed and cultivated in this way, then, monk, you should develop this concentration with initial and sustained thought; you should develop it without initial thought but with sustained thought; you should develop it without initial and sustained thought; you should develop it with rapture; you should develop it without rapture; you should develop it accompanied by pleasure; you should develop it accompanied by equanimity. Monk, when this concentration of yours is developed and cultivated in this way, then, monk, wherever you go, you will go at ease; wherever you stand, you will stand at ease; wherever you sit, you will sit at ease; wherever you lie down, you will lie down at ease.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.63

item.title: - “Venerable sir, right view — for what purpose is it?” - “Right view, Rādha, is for the purpose of disenchantment.” - “Venerable sir, disenchantment…
item.description:
- “Venerable sir, right view — for what purpose is it?” - “Right view, Rādha, is for the purpose of disenchantment.” - “Venerable sir, disenchantment — for what purpose is it?” - “Disenchantment, Rādha, is for the purpose of dispassion.” - “Venerable sir, dispassion — for what purpose is it?” - “Dispassion, Rādha, is for the purpose of liberation.” - “Venerable sir, liberation — for what purpose is it?” - “Liberation, Rādha, is for the purpose of Nibbāna.” - “Venerable sir, Nibbāna — for what purpose is it?” - “Rādha, you have gone beyond the range of this question. For the purpose of entering Nibbāna, Rādha, is the holy life lived; Nibbāna is its final goal, Nibbāna is its end.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.1
📖 Read this sutta
